This page says what the numbers from spax mean, and what they do not. Each
section answers one question in a few sentences and links to the guide that
shows it in code. The examples use [The Cornwall GP example
data](cornwall-data.html). The `spax()` interface and the allocation model are
experimental and may change in later versions.

```{r packages, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(spax)
library(terra)
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
```

## What an FCA index measures

A floating catchment area (FCA) index is the supply around a place per unit of
the demand that competes for it, with nearer facilities counting for more. Each
facility divides its supply (here GP full-time equivalents, FTE) by the demand
around it (here residents), weighted by travel time, and each place adds up the
ratios of the facilities around it. The result, for example GP FTE per 1,000
residents, measures potential access: it does not say where anyone goes or how
much care they receive. In the enhanced two-step FCA (E2SFCA), the two steps
above with travel-time weights, residents times the index add up to the total
supply of the practices that have at least one resident within reach. [Which
FCA index?](fca-methods.html) shows how much supply each index hands back.

## What the allocation model says

The allocation model, a conditional logit model (CLM), gives each origin a
probability for each facility and for an outside option, the choice of none of
the modeled facilities, and these add up to 1. They are
probabilities under a model that knows only travel time and supply. Demand
times probability gives modeled counts. In Cornwall the outside option is
registration with a practice outside mainland Cornwall, in Devon for example.
Registrations are a stock: who is registered where in July 2026. The model
therefore describes where people are registered, not how often they see a GP.
The code counts the registered mainland residents and those registered at a
mainland practice.

```{r outside}
# Mainland small areas and practices, as plain tables
areas <- cornwall_lsoa |>
  filter(!scilly) |>
  st_drop_geometry()
gp <- cornwall_gp |>
  filter(!scilly) |>
  st_drop_geometry()

# Registered mainland residents, and those registered at mainland practices
at_mainland <- cornwall_flows |>
  filter(lsoa %in% areas$lsoa, practice %in% gp$practice)
registered <- c(
  all = sum(areas$registered),
  at_mainland_practices = sum(at_mainland$patients)
)
registered
```

Only
`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * (1 - registered[["at_mainland_practices"]] / registered[["all"]]))`%
of registered mainland residents are registered elsewhere. The outside option
describes them: it is registration elsewhere, not unmet need. [Where do
residents register?](allocation-workflow.html) fits the model.

## What a fit shows, and what it does not

A fit shows which parameter values bring the modeled counts closest to the
observed ones. Another decay curve can fit almost as well, so compare curves
with `compare_fits()`, which sets such fits side by side.
`check_fit()` sets a fit beside simpler allocations on the same counts: one
with no distance decay and, for facility totals, one in proportion to supply
alone. If a simpler allocation fits almost as well, the counts say little
about travel time. This is common with facility totals, which show how many
people each facility serves but not where they live. The fit searches from
several starting values, and when they reach the same estimate the search is
stable. That does not prove the estimate is the best possible, or that the
data pin it down (identify it). [Where do residents
register?](allocation-workflow.html) runs these checks.

## Decay: chosen or fitted

In an FCA index you choose the decay curve, for example a Gaussian curve with
travel scale σ = 10 minutes, under which a practice 10 minutes away counts
about `r round(100 * exp(-1 / 2))`% as much as one next door. The index changes
with that choice: report it and try other values. In the allocation model σ is
estimated from observed counts, so it describes how quickly registration falls
off with travel time in those data. What σ means depends on the shape of the
curve (the kernel): a scale in travel units for the Gaussian kernel, a rate for
the exponential kernel and an exponent for the power kernel. Compare σ only
between fits with the same kernel. [An FCA index
or an allocation model?](model-choice.html) sets a chosen and a fitted scale
side by side.

## Units, sources and dates

The units and dates you give `prep_data(metadata = )` are labels. spax keeps
them with the data and its results, but it does not convert units or check
that they fit together. A Gaussian σ is in the unit of travel, and the units
of supply and demand set the unit of an index. The Cornwall inputs come from
different sources and dates, and their totals differ:

```{r sources}
# Residents of Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly in three sources
pop <- read_spax_example("cornwall_pop.tif")
residents <- c(
  worldpop_2020 = round(global(pop, "sum", na.rm = TRUE)[[1]]),
  ons_mid_2024 = sum(cornwall_lsoa$pop),
  registered_july_2026 = sum(cornwall_lsoa$registered)
)
residents
```

The grid holds
`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * (1 - residents[["worldpop_2020"]] / residents[["ons_mid_2024"]]))`%
fewer residents than the ONS estimate, and the practice registers
`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * (residents[["registered_july_2026"]] / residents[["ons_mid_2024"]] - 1))`%
more. Choose one source of demand for an analysis and say which. The FCA maps
in these guides use the grid. The allocation fits on small areas, and the
comparison in [An FCA index or an allocation model?](model-choice.html), use
the registered residents. [The Cornwall GP example data](cornwall-data.html)
lists the sources.

## Scenarios

A scenario changes an input, for example closes a practice, and runs the model
again with its parameters held at the fitted values. The difference between the
two runs is what the model implies if everyone chooses by the same rule as
before. It is a model-based comparison, not an estimate of what would happen,
and it has no interval. The bootstrap gives one only for a model fitted to
facility totals (see [Uncertainty](#uncertainty)). [What if a practice
closed?](scenario.html) runs one.

## Uncertainty

`bootstrap_fit()` gives intervals for the fitted parameters, for the share of
demand that reaches a facility and for the change a supply scenario makes. It
needs the CLM with a fitted outside weight v0, the pull of the outside option
(`spec_clm()` with its default `outside = "fit"`). The model must be fitted to
facility totals with `obs_totals()`, its default Poisson loss and no outside
count. A fit to flows, such as the Cornwall fit, is outside the method. It also
needs a declaration of how the counts arose:
what was counted, over what period, and that facilities were sampled
independently. That declaration, the observation law, is an assumption the
data cannot confirm, and the intervals hold demand, supply and travel fixed.
[How sure are the estimates?](facility-bootstrap.html) shows the bootstrap on
generated data.

## IDs and missing data

spax lines up demand, supply, travel and observations by their IDs.
`prep_data()` takes the origin IDs from the names of demand and the facility
IDs from the column names of travel. Without them it stops, unless you pass
`origin_ids` and `facility_ids`. A supply vector without names is taken in the
order of the travel columns, so name it too.

Demand can be a known zero, unknown (`NA`) or left out on purpose with
`included`, and the prepared data keep the three apart. Unknown demand stops
`prep_data()` unless you set `missing_demand = "exclude"`, which leaves those
areas out and counts them. The code sets one area of each kind:

```{r demand-kinds}
travel <- cornwall_travel[areas$lsoa, gp$practice]
supply <- setNames(gp$gp_fte_extg, gp$practice)

# One area with no residents, one with unknown demand, one left out on purpose
demand_gaps <- setNames(areas$registered, areas$lsoa)
demand_gaps[1] <- 0
demand_gaps[2] <- NA
included <- names(demand_gaps) != areas$lsoa[3]
prep_data(demand_gaps, supply, travel, missing_demand = "exclude", included = included)
```

Only the `r sum(demand_gaps > 0 & included, na.rm = TRUE)` active areas, with
known positive demand and not left out, enter the model. The print counts the
other three separately. In travel, `Inf` marks a pair known to have no link and
`NA` an unknown time. On numeric data, `prep_data()` stops at unknown travel
unless you set `missing_travel = "omit"`, which leaves those pairs out.
An FCA index on a grid drops unknown times from its sums, so an unknown time
counts as no access. Mask such cells first if they are not truly unreachable.
[Bringing your own data](data-prep.html) shows both.

## Which functions may change

The one-call FCA functions `spax_2sfca()`, `spax_e2sfca()` and `spax_m2sfca()`,
the building blocks shown in [Inside the E2SFCA calculation](e2sfca-steps.html)
and the grid helpers such as `transform_demand()` are stable. The others may
change: `spax()` and `prep_data()`, the `spec_*()`, `decay_*()` and `obs_*()`
functions, `spax_huff()`, `spax_clm()`, `spax_3sfca()`, `spax_huff2sfca()`,
`calc_travel_time()`, `calc_demand()`, the allocation steps listed in the
[Function map](function-naming.html), `check_fit()`, `compare_fits()` and
`bootstrap_fit()`. Record the spax version with every result, for example
with `packageVersion("spax")`.

## Keeping results

Save an allocation result with `saveRDS()`, which keeps the model, its data,
the observations and the fit together. A table from `as.data.frame()` keeps
only the numbers. An FCA result on a grid holds rasters that `saveRDS()` cannot
keep, so save it with `save_spax()` and read it back with `read_spax()`.
[Where do residents register?](allocation-workflow.html) saves a fit and its
tables.
